title: Foreign Investor Flows Near Historic Lows as Jio BlackRock Flags Contrarian Opportunity in Indian Equities
excerpt: FII holdings have dropped to a 14-year low of 15.88%, but the return of inflows in July and valuations at long-term averages suggest the worst may be over, a new report says.
body:
• Foreign institutional investor holdings in Indian equities fell to a 14-year low of 15.88% as of June 30, 2026, with FIIs pulling out ₹1.43 lakh crore during the quarter
  • Jio BlackRock Asset Management's August outlook notes that FII flows returned in July after months of heavy outflows, suggesting improving sentiment
  • India's 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio has returned to its 10-year average of about 20 times, from a sustained premium earlier this year
  • SEBI is planning reforms including lower collateral requirements and easier short-selling to stem foreign capital flight and boost India's MSCI weighting

Foreign investor sentiment toward Indian equities may be approaching an inflection point, according to Jio BlackRock Asset Management, which flagged the return of foreign institutional investor inflows in July as an early sign that the worst of a prolonged withdrawal could be over.

In its August macroeconomic outlook published this week, Jio BlackRock noted that foreign investor flows into India are near historical lows — but pointed out that similar troughs in the past have been followed by recoveries in both flows and market performance. The observation amounts to a contrarian setup for investors willing to look past the near-term pessimism.

The Scale of the Retreat

The numbers underscore just how dramatic the foreign pullback has been. FII ownership of Indian equities fell to 15.88% as of June 30, 2026, down from 16.12% in March and the lowest level in 14 years, according to PRIME Database Group. Foreign investors pulled out ₹1.43 lakh crore during the June quarter alone, with secondary market outflows of ₹1.53 lakh crore partially offset by primary market inflows.

Over the past three years, 41 out of 50 Nifty-50 stocks saw net FII selling, signaling a macro-level decision to reduce India allocations. IT, BFSI, and FMCG bore the brunt, with combined outflows exceeding $19 billion over 12 months.

India's weighting in the MSCI emerging markets index has fallen below 12%, from a peak of 21% in September 2024.

Domestic Investors Fill the Gap

As foreign money has flowed out, domestic institutional investors have stepped in with remarkable consistency. Domestic mutual fund holdings rose for the twelfth consecutive quarter to a record 11.58%, driven by monthly SIP inflows of approximately ₹30,000 crore.

"For years, FIIs had been the largest non-promoter shareholder category in the Indian market with their investment decisions having a huge bearing on the overall direction of the market. This is no longer the case."

— Pranav Haldea, Managing Director, PRIME Database Group

In what JM Financial characterized as near-perfect counter-absorption, domestic institutions increased their stakes in 39 out of 41 Nifty stocks where FIIs sold. The combined share of DIIs, retail investors, and high-net-worth individuals reached an all-time high of 28.66%.

Valuations Reset to Long-Term Averages

The Jio BlackRock report highlighted a key valuation shift. India's 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio has returned to its 10-year average of approximately 20 times after trading at a sustained premium. India's valuation relative to broader emerging markets has also fallen back to its long-term average of around 1.4 times.

However, the report flagged risks. Urban and rural consumer confidence has fallen to its lowest level since September 2023, which could weigh on discretionary spending and corporate earnings growth.

Regulatory Reform in the Works

India's markets regulator SEBI is planning reforms to reverse foreign capital flight, Reuters reported this week. The changes include lowering collateral requirements in cash equities, encouraging longer-dated derivatives, and making stock short-selling easier. SEBI plans to roll out the changes within nine months.

Separately, India's longer-term manufacturing opportunity remains intact. Citing Morgan Stanley projections, Jio BlackRock noted that manufacturing gross value added could rise from $519 billion in 2025 to $1.5 trillion by 2035 in the base case.

Whether the early improvement in foreign flows develops into a sustained reversal remains the key question for Indian markets heading into the second half of 2026.
